concept.name: Trading plan
concept.definition: A written document specifying in advance what will be traded, under which setups and conditions, with what entry, exit, sizing, and risk rules, and how performance will be reviewed. It converts trading from ad hoc reaction into an explicit, testable procedure and is a foundational tool of trading discipline.
concept.intuition: The plan is the contract you sign with yourself before emotions show up: it answers every 'what now?' question before the market asks it.
concept.mechanics: Typically contains instruments and sessions traded, setup definitions with entry and exit criteria, position-sizing and risk limits (per-trade, daily, total), invalidation conditions, and a review cadence. Its function is pre-commitment: moving decisions to a calm design phase so that in-session behavior is execution, not improvisation.
concept.failure_modes: Plans fail when they are vague ('buy strength'), when they encode no real edge, or when they are rewritten mid-session under stress. Over-specified plans also break at regime changes they did not anticipate.
concept.misconceptions: A plan is not a prediction and need not forecast the market; it is a decision procedure. Nor is having ideas the same as having a plan - unwritten, untested rules cannot be followed or evaluated.
concept.example: A trader's plan says: only momentum setups on gapping large-caps, risk 0.5% per trade, stop at the premarket low, maximum three trades daily - so a midday FOMO urge to buy a random mover is answered by the document, not the mood.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
